item.title: Hegseth calls rare press conference ahead of expected impeachment resolution in Congress
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Facing an expected impeachment resolution in Congress, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said he’s eager to litigate the policy choices that he and President Donald Trump have made in Iran and Venezuela. “If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you’re taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic,” Hegseth told reporters Monday. He also announced that he would hold a press conference on Tuesday — his first in over 180 days — on the looming impeachment threat. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie has pushed the impeachment resolution forward over the objections of House GOP leadership as momentum grows to hold Hegseth accountable for the Iran war, which many Republicans blame for the party’s midterm election wipeout. Hegseth argued that starting the war with Iran was a “bold move” by Trump “and as the president points out so clearly -- you can’t let crazy Islamists have a nuclear bomb.” “The choice was don’t act and wish it away or take a bold move, which the president did with Midnight Hammer, which we’ve done with Epic Fury,” Hegseth said, referring to the code names for the strike on Iranian nuclear facilities and the larger war. Hegseth's public defense of the war comes after voters last week overwhelmingly showed the unpopularity of the conflict. According to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States, about 6 in 10 said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, though the survey suggested the Iran war was not the top issue for most voters. Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to shaping how they voted for Congress. That was well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption. item.title: Hegseth impeachment push looms as Congress returns for a busy lame-duck session
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Following the historic midterm election sweeping Democrats into majority control of the House and Senate , Congress returns Monday for a five-week lame-duck session, with a long to-list to tackle before the end of the year and dozens of lawmakers ending their tenure in the House, and at least 17 senators heading home as well. The lame-duck session kicks off Monday with a two-week legislative period wrapped with freshman orientation for members-elect who will be seated in the 120th Congress on Jan. 3. There are still several races that are too close to call, but as it stands Friday, at least 109 incoming House freshmen will be seated -- the largest pre-convening freshmen class in the lower chamber in almost 100 years -- since the 73rd Congress convened in 1933. Umit Bektas/Reuters - PHOTO: The US Capitol building in Washington, November 4, 2026. On the floor, House Speaker Mike Johnson is already hearing it from his own conference after GOP leadership plans to advance just one piece of legislation under a rule next week -- continuing the frustrations voiced by some of his members earlier this fall when the speaker dismissed lawmakers for a six-week campaign blitz rather than put Republican legislative wins on the floor. Massie pushes for Hegseth impeachment Johnson's designs for the lame-duck session could be quickly derailed as Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, who lost a GOP primary months ago, is expected to reintroduce a privileged resolution to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth . Massie has a resolution with eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, who is staring down consternation at both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue in the wake of Tuesday's Democratic victories. President Donald Trump said Thursday he intends to keep Hegseth in his job amid assessments from several Republicans -- including Vice President JD Vance -- that the Iran war led to the party's midterm losses. Trump says he has 'every intention' to keep Hegseth In a video posted Thursday, Hegseth proclaimed that he will not back down -- doubling down on the Iran war and his cultural agenda at the Pentagon while drawing a parallel to Trump. "This is not about me, but of course the other side, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democratic allies has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly. Just like they tried against President Trump twice." Massie could move as early as Monday, teeing up a showdown midweek on Hegseth impeachment. Epstein files 2.0 Speaking of Massie, the president’s primary intraparty detractor is on the brink of having his latest Epstein discharge petition ripen with 218 signatures -- this effort squarely aimed at Attorney General Todd Blanche. Massie already has amassed 216 signatures, including four fellow lame-duck GOP signatures (himself, Reps. Nancy Mace, Ralph Norman and Brian Fitzpatrick) on the petition. Much to the chagrin of Speaker Johnson, Massie now needs just two more Democrats to endorse the petition to force floor consideration of the Epstein Transparency Act II -- a bill that empowers state attorneys general, victims and members of Congress to sue the U.S. Attorney General in federal court for unlawfully withholding or redacting Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell investigative records. In response to allegations that Blanche and other department officials deliberately mishandled the release of millions of files from the Justice Department’s past investigations of deceased convicted sex offender Epstein, the attorney general acknowledged "mistakes" in failing to properly redact certain names of some victims but testified that the department immediately sought to fix those issues. "Whenever we learned that any victim's name had been improperly non-redacted, we immediately took the document down and fixed it as soon as we could," Blanche testified July 15 at the Senate Judiciary Committee. "That doesn't excuse the mistakes of which I take full responsibility, but it does mean that we tried to fix them. We -- we complied with the act." Election 2026 live results New GOP leadership elections Johnson announced he won't run for GOP leader in the next Congress, pitting Majority Leader Steve Scalise against Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan in a race for House Republican leader on Tuesday. Meanwhile, House Democrats have set their leadership elections for Nov. 18, when Hakeem Jeffries is expected to secure the speaker nomination from the Democratic caucus. Tom Brenner/Getty Images - PHOTO: Volunteers applaud as US House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries gives a thumbs up at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee midterm election night phone bank and watch party at a hotel in Washington, November 3, 2026. Senate Republicans are currently scheduled to hold closed-door election to select their party leaders on Tuesday morning. All current members of the Senate GOP leadership team are seeking to retain their positions, and no major shake-ups are expected at this time. Still, things could change as people close to Trump question whether an overhaul is needed. Only the remaining incumbents and newly elected incoming Republican senators will vote in that secret ballot, closed-door leadership election. Outgoing members will not. Democratic leadership has not yet announced a date for their leadership elections as Chuck Schumer lines up support for majority leader. Freshmen orientation House new-member orientation kicks off on Sunday with events scheduled throughout the week, highlighted by a new member photo opportunity on the House steps on Thursday morning. Senate new-member orientation is also scheduled for the first half of the week, when members-elect are also expected to be on the Hill. 'Extinction-level event,' 'blue tsunami': How Republicans eyeing 2028 are taking midterm losses In the Senate, at least 17 senators are leaving, bringing in a new generation of freshmen to take the oath. Even more new members will join the ranks eventually as incumbent senators Marsha Blackburn and Amy Klobuchar head to their respective state's governor mansions and appoint their successors. The Alaska and Mississippi Senate races have yet to be projected, but Democratic wins in those states would further grow the Senate freshmen class. Legislative to-do list The challenges facing the lame-duck Congress are stacking up. Government funding runs out after Dec. 11 and lawmakers are far from striking a deal to avert a government shutdown. The House and Senate must pass the National Defense Authorization Act, the annual Pentagon policy bill, before the end 2026. Disputes about funding for the war in Iran could come to a head as the deadline to pass the bill approaches. Reauthorizing Section 702 of Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) and passing the expired Farm Bill are also on lawmakers' long to-do list. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images - PHOTO: The sun sets on the U.S. Capitol on Election Day evening on November 3, 2026 in Washington. Senate Republicans will also attempt to move quickly to confirm Trump’s remaining nominees before losing control of the chamber in January -- challenging Republican Sen. John Thune to schedule sufficient floor time to overcome Democrats who may be unwilling to agree to unanimous consent time agreements during the lame-duck session. Senators will also continue consideration of permitting reform legislation, the bipartisan package overhauling federal laws and regulations to streamline infrastructure projects. On Monday, the Senate will hold a procedural vote -- which will provide an indication of whether the negotiations that were gaining steam ahead of the midterm recess will hold, or if Democrats seek to punt the issue to the next Congress when in majority control. This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/Politics/congress-returns-crowded-lame-duck-session-hegseth-impeachment/story?id=137918357

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries has a choice to make: Will he work with Trump?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump said after Tuesday’s midterm drubbing he wants to “work with” Democrats. Now Hakeem Jeffries has to decide if his party will play ball. As he prepares to lead a massive House Democratic majority, perhaps the presumptive speaker's toughest call will be how to handle Trump. After years of dismissing and denigrating the president, Jeffries has to weigh varying opinions inside his caucus: Some, including incoming red-district freshmen, want to attempt collaboration, while plenty of others want total war. Trump is already testing Democrats by appointing Stephen Miller, one of their top administration boogeymen, as his new White House chief of staff — prompting a characteristically fierce reply from Jeffries denouncing Miller as a “dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist” whose “presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.” But members close to Jeffries acknowledge he might soon have to strike a different tone as Democrats pledge to make good on their campaign promises to lower costs ahead of 2028 — or at least be seen trying. Rep. Greg Meeks of New York, a longtime confidant of the Democratic leader, said in an Election Day interview that Jeffries has “always been willing to sit down and talk and to negotiate.” “It has been the other side that has rejected us and called names … tweeting nasty things and cussing at folks and not being an individual who can respect the office of the presidency,” he continued. “Hakeem Jeffries will be that individual.” Meeks is not alone in suggesting Jeffries could enter dealmaker mode. It is one of two potential avenues House Democrats are pitching for how he should navigate Trump. The other, preferred by many progressives, involves Jeffries leading House Democrats in passing bills without compromising with the White House, then daring the president to veto them — matching the aggressive plan by Jeffries and fellow Democrats to use their new subpoena powers to investigate Trump, his administration and his allies. In the wake of Democrats’ massive midterm victory — which could secure them as many as 260 seats — Jeffries has previewed elements of both strategies. Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Jeffries said Democrats have “consistently made the point that we are ready, willing, and able to find bipartisan common ground with the other side of the aisle as long as we can bring about meaningful change on the issues that matter, and that begins with decisively addressing the affordability crisis.” But that doesn’t mean there has been proactive outreach: Jeffries had not spoken with Trump as of Sunday morning, he said in an ABC News interview. A White House spokesperson, Lauren Bis, said Trump is “willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans” but that if “Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.” Jeffries tangled with Trump repeatedly as minority leader, with the two frequently trading barbs on social media. During last year’s funding fight, Jeffries showed his willingness to wage war with the administration by refusing to deliver Democratic votes to fund the government without extensions of Affordable Care Act tax credits or an end to mass deportation funding. At one point, Trump posted a video depicting Jeffries in a sombrero — suggesting he was more interested in protecting undocumented Latino immigrants than Americans. Jeffries called the post “racist” and “bigoted.” Trump has a much less familiar personal relationship with Jeffries than with Sen. Chuck Schumer — Jeffries’ Senate counterpart as Democratic leader and fellow New Yorker. “I’ve seen Donald Trump work with his opponents. He will find something that he can do, something that he agrees with them on,” said Michael Caputo, a longtime Trump adviser who added that the president “will surprise people with the way he’s going to try to work positively in the present environment.” But Friday’s move to elevate Miller sent another message — that Trump has no plans to back off that aggressive agenda that Democrats find toxic, to say nothing of his dramatic expansions of executive power to sidestep opposition in Congress. Jeffries faces inevitable standoffs with the administration over government spending deadlines — including a fight as soon as Dec. 11 over blocking Iran war funding. He will also have to head off a U.S. debt default , predicted to occur some time between next summer and early 2028. During Nancy Pelosi’s speakership, the House and the Trump administration did work out some agreements, most notably to raise the debt ceiling in July 2019. But deals were otherwise scarce. In 2019, the House passed about 400 bills that died in the Republican-controlled Senate or at the president’s desk. Jeffries will have a hefty Senate majority to work with, but a former Democratic aide from that period, who like others in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly, called the dynamic between a Democratic speaker and Trump “a very challenging, nuanced line to walk,” and post-election comments from lawmakers underscored that challenge. “We need to compromise, but we're not going to compromise our values,” Rep. Greg Stanton of Arizona, a senior member of the centrist New Democrat Coalition, said in an interview last week. “But we are going to have to reach agreement and meet halfway in order to get things done.” That’s a sentiment shared by several incoming members who won historically Republican districts and now want to deliver affordability wins to campaign on in 2028. Asked about how House Democrats should navigate the Trump relationship, Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke of Wisconsin emphasized a need for collaboration on improving people’s livelihoods. “People are really struggling here and hanging on by a thread, and I think I really worked to build a broad coalition within my candidacy and my campaign, uniting people of all political stripes to vote for me,” she said in a Thursday interview. But Democrats have shown there is a limit to their appetite for engagement with Trumpworld. After the New York Times disclosed over the summer that Jeffries accepted a meeting with Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, to discuss affordability issues, many Democrats were surprised and upset. But the cozy-up approach has worked for at least one prominent Democratic leader, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has seemingly charmed the president — even while criticizing his administration — and says he will work with Trump to lower costs. But several progressives are suggesting a different vision of the relationship with Trump and are reluctant to compromise on their ambitious legislative agenda to accommodate the president or other Republicans. Hard-left Rep.-elect William Lawrence of Michigan said in an interview, “We’ll have to put the ball in the president’s court to see what he does.” “We should be putting bills on his desk to lower costs and to end the war,” he said. “And I hope that he will sign those bills, but we should push him to do so and make clear that Democrats are here to legislate on behalf of the American people and advance popular policies.” The likely next head of the Congressional Black Caucus, Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, proposed a similar approach: “We're going to put things on his desk, and we're going to call him out, and we're going to invite the American people to watch,” he said in a post-election interview. “Sign it or veto it, Mr. President. Show the American people where you really stand.” But other Democrats say they can only game out their strategy so far. As the Miller pick — and the furious Democratic reaction to it — underscored, Trump’s posture toward governing will influence how Jeffries and his party respond. “That depends on the president, right?” Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado said Wednesday when asked in an interview about navigating Trump. “We have always said that our job is to protect America, to make Americans' lives better, and that we will always have a discussion about how to do that if they're willing to do it. They're the ones that shut the door.” Lisa Kashinsky, Megan Messerly, Calen Razor and Kelsey Brugger contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/09/hakeem-jeffries-trump-relationship-01155108

item.title: Trump says his deportation policy ‘might have been too tough’ for voters in the election
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In an interview with 60 Minutes , President Trump said his administration's hardline approach to immigration enforcement around deportations may have been "too tough" in pursuing people in the country for a decade or more. The president spoke with 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat three days after Republicans faced jarring losses in the midterm elections. Support for the party plummeted in South Texas and other heavily Latino areas that trended toward the GOP two years ago — a reversal that many voters linked at least in part to Mr. Trump's immigration crackdown. Mr. Trump said his immigration crackdown "both helped and hurt" him at the polls. He believes he "got an A+ for closing up the border," and got "very high marks for getting the bad ones out." "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally," the president continued. "Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes." He continued: "I think it was too tough." "A lot of people would say that it's great, but a lot of people think it's too tough," he said. The president also said he'd "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate starting next year. It's unclear whether the Trump administration is planning to alter its immigration enforcement strategy. On Friday, Mr. Trump replaced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, a hardliner who is widely viewed as an architect of the Trump administration's immigration policies. The president's 2024 victory was fueled partly by voters' discontent with former President Joe Biden's immigration policies, including the surge in unauthorized U.S.-Mexico border crossings. Since Mr. Trump's return to the White House, illegal border crossings have fallen dramatically . Federal officials have also ramped up arrests and deportations in the interior of the country, with the number of people detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement charting record highs. Miller pushed the agency to aim for 3,000 arrests per day last year. A large share of the arrestees do not have criminal records beyond immigration offenses. The Trump administration has long said its priority is to arrest the "worst first," while warning that anybody who is in the U.S. illegally can be arrested and deported. And many of the administration's immigration tactics have drawn scrutiny, including its citywide crackdowns in Minneapolis and elsewhere , its vehicle stops , its detention practices and its practice of deporting some migrants to places other than their home country. Some Republicans have pushed back, with Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar of South Florida warning in September that many Hispanics who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 "feel betrayed." In exit polling , 58% think the Trump administration's actions on immigration have gone too far. Still, on the question of which party voters think is better able to handle immigration, voters trust Republicans (43%) slightly more than Democrats (41%). The administration has defended its approach, saying it is targeting public safety threats. Read the full transcript and watch an extended version of the interview here. item.title: Biden says Trump's Jan. 6 actions 'should follow him to his grave'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Former President Joe Biden also wrote in his memoir that Trump 'led an insurrection.' (Brent Stirton / Getty) Former President Joe Biden issued scathing criticism of President Donald Trump in his forthcoming memoir, saying his actions during the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol “should follow him to his grave.” Biden’s comments, published as a book excerpt in The Atlantic on Monday, mark some of his strongest criticism of Trump since the former president left office. In the excerpt, Biden says Trump “led an insurrection” and slammed his decision to issue sweeping pardons of Jan. 6 defendants. Trump and Biden at Trump's inauguration ceremony at the Capitol in 2025. (Chip Somodevilla / Getty) “The criminals who attacked law-enforcement officers that day didn’t deserve pardons,” Biden wrote. “They deserved prison terms.” The former president added that Trump and the president’s supporters “continue to preen and posture like they’re supporters of law enforcement.” “Here’s my view: You don’t get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement,” he wrote. “What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave.” Reached for comment, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis called Biden “the worst president in American history.” She pointed to his handling of the border, crime and inflation, adding, “What they did to this country should never be forgotten.” The memoir, “Promise Me, America,” is set to be published on Nov. 17. In a September interview with Time magazine, Trump acknowledged that he was considering pardoning members of his administration before his term concluded, pointing to Biden’s decision to issue preemptive pardons. Biden issued those pardons to his son, Hunter Biden , and other members of his family, lawmakers on the congressional Jan. 6 committee, Dr. Anthony Fauci, and former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Mark Milley. Biden also described his meeting with Trump after the 2024 election, part of a tradition where the outgoing president briefs the incoming president. Biden said that Trump’s tone “bordered on fawning” and said that Trump told him that “if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends” — a remark that the former president said left him “too stunned to respond.” “He said my performance on job creation had been ‘extraordinary,’” Biden wrote. “He added that he’d been relieved he didn’t have to run against me. I didn’t really understand why he was buttering me up, so I cut off his compliments to move on to the business at hand.” During the approximately two hour meeting, Biden said that he wanted to give Trump an overview of world issues that he believed would “dominate his presidency.” “He nodded appreciatively,” Biden said of Trump. “But I noticed a curious pattern: He focused on the personalities of the leaders, as if we were sharing gossip about people at a dinner party, not discussing issues of global significance.” Biden announced Sunday that he would not “be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped,” pointing to his fight against cancer. “Some days are better than others,” Biden said in the post to X. “It hasn’t stopped me. item.title: Senate Republicans return to Capitol furious with Trump after big losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Senate Republicans returning to the Capitol on Monday are furious with President Trump, whom they blame for last week's big losses in Senate and House races. The anger is raising the chances that the party could pivot away from the lame-duck president in the lead-up to the 2028 presidential election, according to GOP aides and strategists. Tensions are also rising with Trump’s Friday announcement that immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller will be his new chief of staff, replacing the outgoing Susie Wiles. The Miller appointment suggests a doubling down on the president’s policies, particularly on immigration enforcement, after an election in which Hispanic voters swung decisively toward Democrats, especially in Texas. Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) on Sunday said Miller should be fired, not promoted. “If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people,” Stutzman said in an interview on CNN. “You don’t promote those who are — who were in charge of what was supposed to be delivered.” Whit Ayres, a prominent Republican pollster, said Senate Republicans will be less deferential to Trump after suffering a huge loss of seats in last week’s election. Ayres said Trump “clearly will remain the leader of the party for the next two years, but I also think the knee-jerk obeisance to whatever his whims are at the moment is likely over.” “There is so much resentment particularly among Republicans in the Senate for what Donald Trump did in North Carolina and South Carolina and Texas,” he said, referring to Trump’s endorsement of candidates Michael Whatley, Darline Graham and Ken Paxton, who all lost by large margins in the general election. “I think his iron grip over the Senate Republicans is likely to be loosened,” Ayres said. One senior Senate Republican aide predicted GOP senators and the broader party will begin to shift away from Trump over the next year. “Trump said he was on the ballot. He wasn’t on the ballot but acted like he was on the ballot,” and “a lot of people” voted as if Trump was atop the GOP ticket when they voted for Democrats in battleground states around the country, the aide said. “We need somebody who can work together with people, who doesn’t just try to divide — who is focused on real issues that people care about that are of importance versus stupid little internet memes, which it seems like Trump and Vance are more focused on now,” the aide argued. Republican sources say Trump undermined their chances of winning key Senate races by endorsing weak candidates, such as Paxton and Graham, and by failing to adhere to any message discipline. GOP senators are also frustrated by what they saw as Trump’s reluctance to spend from his massive campaign war chest until late in the campaign. Senate Republican aides and pollsters say Trump's dismal influence on races across the country will spark an intense discussion about what's next for the party and whether it's time to turn the page on MAGA and its policies. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and members of his leadership team lobbied Trump for months to back Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) over Paxton, the state attorney general, in the Texas Senate Republican primary — or to at least stay neutral — but Trump ignored their advice and endorsed Paxton before the primary runoff, sinking Cornyn’s chances. Thune and his leadership team urged the president and Senate GOP colleagues to keep their political messaging focused on their legislative accomplishments, especially the popular tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, such as its tax deductions for tips. But Trump instead often veered off from the plan, getting into fights over the White House ballroom, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the Kennedy Center, the East Potomac Park golf course and other topics that GOP strategists viewed as unhelpful to delivering the broader Republican message. Trump blamed last week’s losses on poor Republican candidates, but many Senate Republicans think the blame for the loss of at least seven seats lies squarely with the unpopular president. “We’re up here talking about the generational benefits of avoiding a $4 trillion-plus tax hike and everything else that’s inside that bill, and then the president is talking about the Reflecting Pool or the ballroom, and those are the things that get the headlines,” a Senate GOP aide said. “Message synchronization was off.” Senate Republicans were galled when Trump dismissed the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act as a “big yawn.” GOP leaders were touting the bipartisan legislation as a major accomplishment to address housing affordability, but Trump popped their balloon as he said he cared more about passing the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, a package to overhaul election rules that had virtually no chance of passing Congress. Senate Republican sources also said Trump waited too long to spend the hundreds of millions of dollars he stockpiled ahead of the midterm elections. “They sat on that $400 million until it was too late to start spending it,” a second GOP aide said. Trump said in August he would spend “a lot” of money from a pro-Trump super PAC to help “good” GOP candidates, but Senate GOP strategists complained the president’s political allies waited until the final weeks of the campaign to dump money into races, which diluted their firepower because they had to pay higher television ad rates. Trump announced in late October that he would end up spending more than $400 million by Election Day to help Republicans keep Congress. When Republicans got blown out on Election Day, the White House blamed GOP candidates for not putting in as much effort as the president to promote their candidacies and records. Trump declared on election night: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Senate Republicans say they think Trump also hurt them by constantly bashing their failure to pass the SAVE America Act, even after Republicans held at least five votes on the legislation, either in whole or in part, and came nowhere close to collecting the 60 votes the bill needed to advance. Trump warned Senate Republicans would be “in big trouble” if they didn’t abolish the filibuster to ram the bill through the chamber. “When you’re casting your own teammate as the opponent, what message does that send to the voter?” the GOP aide said. A third Senate Republican aide argued that Trump clearly deserves the blame for the loss of seven — and maybe as many as nine — Senate seats and more than 40 House seats. “Trump’s message was, ‘I’m going to deliver you a good economy,’ and it seems like the only person who benefited from the economy was him,” the aide said, adding that Democrats successfully tied together voters’ concerns about rising prices and corruption in Washington. “Those two things led to a disaster with independents,” the aide said. And then he attacked Iran, and we're still in it,” he told SiriusXM’s “The John Kasich Show.” “This president ran on and won on a platform of drain the swamp, right? … And now it seems like he or his family is in on every transaction and deal that goes on in Washington,” he said. “And those two things, I think, caused people to say, ‘You know, I just can't vote for a Republican while he's still in office.’” Cornyn argued Trump “misread his mandate” after the 2024 election. item.description:

Nvidia's board of directors said Sunday it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang being the target of an alleged Chinese spy, with whom he had an affair. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia employees and is cooperating with the investigation. Reports have identified Alice Huang (no relation), former executive at tech firm Megaspeed, as the person he had the relationship with. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Jensen Huang said in a statement. If you haven't been following the stock market closely, you may not be familiar with Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies. And you may be wondering why U.S. security officials would be concerned about a CEO's extramarital affair. Here's what we know so far, and why this tech CEO's affair is a big deal. First, who is Jensen Huang? Jensen Huang is the CEO of Nvidia, one of the biggest makers of specialized computer chips in the world. Its chips were initially designed for computer graphics, but with the AI boom of the past few years, demand for Nvidia's hardware has skyrocketed. China and the U.S. are in a heated competition for AI technology, and that includes access to chips like the ones Nvidia makes. Jensen Huang is an American citizen who was born in Taiwan. He founded Nvidia in 1993 and has been the company's president and CEO since, steering the company through the AI boom of the past several years. What we know about the affair so far According to the New York Times, it's unclear when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang — an alleged Chinese spy — but the two were photographed together in 2024 at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan. It was roughly around that time when Megaspeed, the AI company she worked for, began its push into the AI sector. Multiple news reports were unable to confirm if Alice Huang is still employed at Megaspeed today. Megaspeed has touted its membership in Nvidia's partnership program, which would provide access to its latest technology. Huang apologized for the affair in a message to Nvidia employees, and asked for privacy for his family. "I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused," Huang wrote, "and I accept the criticism that comes with it." He pledged to earn back his employees' confidence, and added that he was cooperating fully with the board's investigation. "I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," he wrote. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was gathering information for the Chinese government. China denied that it was spying , calling the allegation unsubstantiated. "It is nothing but smears against China," a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson said. The New York Times also reported that executives at Nvidia contacted the U.S. Commerce Department last year seeking information about the department's investigation into Megaspeed. The investigation was later transferred to the Department of Justice, which is reportedly looking into Megaspeed's involvement in potentially illegally routing Nvidia products into China. Why this matters AI is the biggest thing in tech right now, infiltrating our lives via chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude, and disrupting all sorts of industries from software development and bioengineering. Governments are trying to determine how and when to use AI for security and across business sectors too. China and the U.S. are hastily competing to dominate AI development for uses across multiple industries. The development has been so rapid that some CEOs of AI companies have suggested a pause may be in order before the technology develops beyond what humans can control. Nvidia has contracts with the U.S. government to use its technology in several areas , and Jensen Huang has a close relationship with President Trump. U.S. officials are trying to determine if the affair may have allowed the Chinese government to receive information about Nvidia's technology and its agreements with the U.S. government. Nvidia's board said in its statement that the company does not believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. President Trump said late Sunday that he considers Huang "a fine person" who should stay on as CEO of Nvidia. "I think he probably has an excuse for it. We'll have to hear it," Trump told reporters Sunday night. "He's done an amazing job for our country." item.title: Trump questions midterm results days after congratulating Democrats
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump speaks with reporters before boarding Air Force One, at President Donald J. Trump International Airport in West Palm Beach, Florida, on Nov. 8, 2026. —Jaquelyn Martin—AP President Donald Trump questioned the integrity of the midterm elections on Monday, less than a week after the Republican Party suffered historic defeats in both swing states and former GOP strongholds . “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” Trump asked in a Truth Social post early Monday. “How could the Polls be so wrong???” “Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote,” he continued, adding: “It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” His post did not elaborate on what was meant by the statement. Read more: Welcome to Trump’s Lame-Duck Era Trump’s unsubstantiated fraud claims come nearly two weeks after he told reporters on Oct. 27 that he would respect the election results “if they’re honest elections.” As results came in throughout Nov. 3 and into Nov. 4, Trump seemed to accept the outcome. “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country,” Trump told CBS News in an election-night phone call. It was a sentiment he repeated in an interview that aired Sunday on 60 Minutes , when he said he would be willing to work with Democrats on immigration, addressing an issue that had been top-of-mind for voters ahead of Election Day. “I think that's something that's actually doable," he said. By Monday morning, however, Trump was casting doubt on the results. The comment harkens back to Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of election interference and ensuing lawsuits after he lost the presidency to Joe Biden in 2020. Trump's history of election denial Trump was sowing doubt on the 2020 election before voting began, telling the public that August that “the only way we’re going to lose this election is if the election is rigged.” Following his loss, Trump refused to concede to Biden. Instead, he began to spread conspiracy theories about widespread election fraud, without evidence. On Nov. 7, 2020, shortly before news organizations projected Biden’s victory, Trump falsely declared on Twitter that he had “WON THIS ELECTION, BY A LOT!” Echoing Trump’s false claims also became a test of loyalty within the Republican Party, with House Speaker Mike Johnson, Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, and former Georgia Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene among those who espoused the false view. Trump and his allies filed 62 lawsuits challenging or seeking to overturn the results between Nov. 4, 2020, and Jan. 6, 2021, according to the House Jan. 6 committee . Only one produced a victory—a narrow Pennsylvania ruling that didn’t establish fraud or change the outcome. Some cases were dismissed on procedural grounds; others failed on the merits. The legal defeats did not stop Trump from repeating his false claims. On Dec. 22, 2020, he alleged on social media that Democrats had “DUMPED HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF BALLOTS IN THE SWING STATES LATE IN THE EVENING.” The claims escalated on Jan. 5, 2021, when Trump tweeted : “Washington is being inundated with people who don’t want to see an election victory stolen by emboldened Radical Left Democrats.” This followed repeated calls for his supporters to descend upon Washington D.C. and protest the results . As Congress met to count and certify the Electoral College votes on Jan. 6, 2021, a mob of Trump supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol. His efforts to overturn his 2020 defeat also led to criminal charges. In August 2023, Special Counsel Jack Smith brought four federal charges against Trump, alleging efforts to subvert the results through pressure on officials, fraudulent elector slates, and interference with certification. Trump pleaded not guilty. On the campaign trail in 2024, he doubled down on his allegations of election interference by urging voters to deliver a victory that was “too big to rig.” The case was dismissed in November that year, after his reelection, because of Justice Department policy against prosecuting a sitting President. item.title: Democrats nearly flipped deep-red states. Some say their own party held them back.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats across the country won upsets despite being vastly outspent by Republicans, sometimes doubly in marquee races. But candidates who narrowly lost in Southern states wonder if that blue wave could have reached them too if only their party's leaders funded them. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. In Florida, the Democratic candidates for Senate and governor who came within several points of victories criticized national Democrats for declining requests to send more money despite signs they could win in a Republican stronghold. Several Louisiana Democrats said the party squandered an opportunity to pull off another Senate win in a state where farmer Jamie Davis lost his race for an open seat by less than two percentage points. Mississippi Senate Democratic candidate Scott Colom, who is narrowly leading with thousands of outstanding ballots and didn't get national party funding until the very end of the campaign, has lamented that Democrats often don't see the state as worth competing in. The disagreement over spending decisions reflects the complicated and at times unpredictable landscape of money in politics. Democrats were able to win in other states despite being significantly outspent by Republicans, including Texas and Ohio. But the difference is the Democrats there still raised and received enough help from outside groups to blanket airwaves and run robust campaigns. With such narrow margins without significant financial support, some of the losing Democratic candidates and their allies say national funding could have closed that final gap to victory. "We missed an historic opportunity," Florida Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly said in a statement. Jolly came within two points of beating Republican Byron Donalds, who raised more than $170 million to the Democrat's more than $26 million. The Democratic Governors Association announced $1 million for Jolly at the end of the campaign, a relative pittance in one of the most expensive states to run advertising statewide. This year's race was a stark contrast to Florida's last governor's race, when Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), who was term-limited this year and is making plans for a 2028 presidential run, won by 20 percentage points. If national investment had come through, Jolly said, "without question we would have won." The DGA declined to comment. Of this year's 36 gubernatorial races, Democrats won 29, meaning the party will lead a majority of states for the first time since 2010. Angie Nixon, the Democratic Senate candidate in Florida, asked supporters after her three percentage-point loss to Sen. Ashley Moody (R) to "imagine what would have happened if we had more investment early on." In September, Nixon told MSNOW she asked Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York) for funding, and he was hesitant. The Democrats' Senate campaign arm ultimately did not spend on her race, though Schumer helped her fundraise last month. Moody had more than 60 times the amount of outside money supporting her, according to the latest FEC filings. National Democrats have made the case that they entered races where their money could go the furthest as the party sought to win back control of Congress. They point to investments elsewhere in the South, made in media markets where it's cheaper to run ads, on races that became suddenly more competitive, such as the Senate campaigns of Annie Andrews in South Carolina and Colom in Mississippi. Other battleground states such as Texas and Ohio where polls showed the Democrats more competitive were expensive to compete in, diverting money that could have been spent elsewhere. Democrats will hold at least 54 Senate seats in January and are leading in the Mississippi and Alaska races that are too close to call. The spending debate also shows the reality of any election - blue wave or not, there are always surprising races or unexpected battlegrounds that can prompt grumblings that more money could've made a difference. Lauren French, a spokesperson for the Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC, said in a statement that the group had spent "every dollar at its disposal to help build the largest Senate majority in decades." She added that their spending helped keep those races competitive even as Republicans spent nearly double across the same states. Steve Schale, a longtime Democratic strategist in Florida, said more money would have helped in races like Nixon's but it's difficult to assess whether it would've led to victory. "It's easy to say if they had just written a larger check," Schale said. "And it's not an unfair criticism, but I also understand that these committees don't have unlimited money." Others who criticize how national Democrats spend their money say the decisions show the weaknesses in their strategy. Some activists and Black Democrats say the party has overlooked the South, including Florida, Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee. The four states were among those where Republicans redrew favorable congressional districts this cycle and would probably target again ahead of 2028. They have large groups of Black voters, who drove Democrats to wins in some tough races this year. Several Democratic candidates came just shy of unseating Republicans in South Florida. In Tennessee, where state Republicans redrew House maps to ensure no Democrat could win, Democrat Victoria Broderick, who raised less than $100,000, is on the verge of ousting Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R), who raised more than $667,000. Democrat Justin Pearson came just shy of defeating Republican Brent Taylor for a redrawn district. In Alabama, Rep. Shomari Figures (D) won reelection in a redrawn district with the support of national Democratic groups. But Doug Jones, a former Democratic senator, lost the race for governor by a surprisingly close four percentage-point margin. "We need to invest in the South people," Joe Trippi, a strategist who has advised Jones, said on X, adding that Democrats have "been fighting to build a competitive party across the South for years. Maybe now the party will listen." In Louisiana, Davis came remarkably close to flipping an open Senate seat. On his own, he raised $5 million to his Republican opponent, Rep. Julia Letlow, who raised $2 million, according to the latest campaign finance filings. As polls began to show a closer race than expected, Louisiana Rep. Troy A. Carter (D) said he had asked national Democrats for $2 million to support Davis during the last three weeks of the campaign. Another sign that Letlow was in trouble came Monday when President Donald Trump held a tele-rally for her. Carter said Democrats sent some money, but it was "not nearly as much as we would have liked." He declined to say to whom he had made the request and where the spending came from. (Late spending is reflected in FEC filings only after the general election.) Carter said the lack of strong spending reflected a long-standing reluctance from Democrats to invest in certain parts of the South. That will need to change, he said, as a score of high-profile Democrats eye the presidency in 2028. "I believed then, and I believe now, that all roads to the White House are through the South," he said. Fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France were affected last month [Getty Images] France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions "at the European level". The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros. Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across several other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked. Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people". He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act". France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added. Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies. Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC. Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime. On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets. More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight. Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss. The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely. Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe. Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland. Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects. In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them. The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations. item.title: Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assaults
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The British former comedian and actor Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three more. Handing down the sentence Monday at Southwark Crown Court in London, judge Joel Bennathan said Brand told a series of lies throughout the trial, adding he had displayed a "casual and arrogant disregard" for women who said 'No' to him. "About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," Bennathan said. "You were clever — and in many people's eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator." He added, "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say 'no' and to demand justice from criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent." Brand was supported in court by his wife, Laura Gallacher, and his father, Ron. He is expected to serve at least two-thirds of that sentence — around seven years — before being eligible for release. Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Nov. 5. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones called Brand a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator" who treated women as a "disposable commodity." "Mr. Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame," Karmy-Jones said. "He used it to facilitate an access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity." Ahead of his sentencing, one woman, who was sexually assaulted by Brand in 2004 or 2005, told the court Monday in her impact statement: "Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse," Sky News reported. Another woman, who was raped by the comedian in 2009 after meeting him at a comedy show in London, said she was "living with trauma." She said his fame made it "difficult to escape reminders of what had happened," Reuters reported. She said she was worried after the attack that she might have HIV, struggled to eat and sleep, took two to three months off work and abandoned the career she had embarked upon. "Although the rape was 17 years ago, she still finds it affects her ability to form new friendships and to know when she can trust people," the judge said. A third woman who was assaulted by Brand while working on a Channel 4 documentary said that, following the attack, she felt like she had "lost my trust in people." Reflecting on the incident, she added: "I felt powerless in that moment." Last week, Megyn Kelly, the former Fox News host, reacted to Brand’s conviction in disbelief. “I don’t believe the charges, and I don’t have to believe them just because a jury came through with the opposite conclusion,” she said in a YouTube livestream . The next day, in a comment on X, Elon Musk described Brand’s conviction for offenses nearly 20 years old as a “ crazy legal standard .” England doesn’t have a statute of limitations for rape or sexual assault. Brand became a household name in the U.K. in the 2000s as a comedian and broadcaster and had well-documented issues with drugs and alcohol. He went on to star in the movies Get Him to the Greek in 2010 and Arthur the following year. He married singer Katy Perry in October 2010, but Brand filed for divorce in December 2011, citing irreconcilable differences. Their divorce was finalized in July 2012. The claims against Brand were made by six different women, spanning from 1999 to 2009. None of the women knew each other, but came forward to police following a TV documentary and press reports in 2023, in which anonymous allegations were made by other women. Laura Brand, the wife of British actor and comedian Russell Brand, arrives at Southwark Crown Court Monday. REUTERS / REUTERS During the trial, the court heard tearful testimony from the six accusers, who are all entitled to lifelong anonymity. According to the Associated Press, the convictions included a rape that took place in 2009, involving a woman who went to Brand's home after meeting him at one of his shows. She said she had engaged in consensual sex, but that Brand then raped her and removed a condom in the process. Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman when he grabbed her breasts at a London bar in 2004. He was also found guilty over an incident in 2009, in which he demanded a woman give him a massage in front of two of his colleagues and then put his head in her groin. A third complaint of sexual assault ended in a guilty verdict when Brand was found guilty of pushing a woman who worked at a radio station up against a wall and forcibly kissing her. Brand denied the charges and said he had never forced anyone to do something against their will. Footage released by London's Metropolitan Police after the verdict shows Brand being interviewed by police in December 2023. "As I've repeatedly stated publicly and written about extensively, I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I've spent years openly denouncing," Brand can be seen saying. "I've never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity." He said he did "not recall the names" of the complainants, or meeting them, adding, "However, it's entirely possible that I may have encountered them and we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that's been since reimagined." Following the verdict, London's Metropolitan Police Service told Yahoo News that Brand, 51, was facing further allegations of rape from two women. "The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations," the force said. Brand has not been charged in relation to these claims. The head of the Met Police, Sir Mark Rowley, has urged any other victims of Brand to contact the police. "There's two more rape allegations that we're looking at. We're encouraging anybody else to come forward if there's any other allegations," he told British media on Nov. 6. He later said that he "wouldn't be surprised if many, many more come forward," adding of the trial, "This shows that powerful people can be brought down so you are safe stepping forward and we will support and try and bring that person to justice." item.title: 8-year-old Haitian boy in federal custody after ICE check-in
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
An 8-year-old Haitian boy who lost Temporary Protected Status earlier this year was taken into federal custody after an immigration check-in, according to local advocates and school officials. The third grader, who attends Fay Elementary School in San Diego, was placed into government custody alone after attending an Immigration and Customs Enforcement appointment with his uncle on Thursday, according to his school district and an advocacy group. “The eight-year-old received a letter to meet with an ICE agent,” the San Diego Unified School District said in a letter to DHS. “His uncle, with whom he’s been living since the child’s father was deported more than a year ago, took him to meet the agent because he did not want to break the law.” New ICE facility to hold families, unaccompanied minors could open in Louisiana next week Advocates and school officials said the boy had been living with his uncle and cousins after his father was deported to Mexico last year. "They did not give the father the opportunity or chance to actually put in place legal guardianship for the kid," said Guerline Jozef, the executive director of the nonprofit Haitian Bridge Alliance. Cody Petterson, a board trustee with the SDUSD, told ABC News the uncle was designated on school records as an authorized caregiver. Charles Reed/ICE - PHOTO: An officer with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Dallas, Texas. A spokesperson for ICE told ABC News in a statement that because the uncle could not establish legal guardianship, agents treated the 8-year-old as an unaccompanied child under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, a federal law that provides protections for unaccompanied immigrant children. The agency did not allege any wrongdoing or abuse by the uncle, but invoked the law to mandate the child's transfer after designating him as an unaccompanied minor. "Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," the spokesperson said. According to the school district and an advocacy group, the 8-year-old remains in ORR custody. It is unclear if he will be removed from the U.S. Jozef called the detention "an excuse for [ICE] to remove the child and potentially put him in deportation proceedings.” Democrats press HHS over legal representation of migrant children “He was dressed very well, and he is very well cared for,” Jozef added. “There's absolutely no reason for them to remove him from the care of his relatives without putting in place proper procedures for him, knowing very well that ICE already deported the father.” In the letter to DHS, San Diego Unified School District officials said they have “witnessed situations in which children who should be attending school and participating in a supportive educational environment instead find themselves in government facilities.” “Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” the district said.
